title: Why You Can Never Precisely Date When Two Languages Split (Swadesh's Math Ceiling)
paper: Evolution of the lexicon: a probabilistic point of view (2510.22220)
pitch: Explainer video walking through the paper's core surprising result: even with zero contamination/borrowing and perfect cognate judgments, there's a hard probabilistic floor on how precisely lexicostatistics can date a language split, because word-replacement is a stochastic process (like radioactive decay with huge variance at short timescales) — and adding a second stochastic process (gradual word *modification*, not just replacement) actually sharpens the estimate. Visualize with a simple binomial/Poisson simulation of vocabulary replacement.
discussion_why: discussion via analogy: it's the same 'small sample, huge variance' trap poker players fall into misreading a hot streak, so it's an easy bridge topic

title: Lexicostatistics Confidence-Interval Simulator
paper: Evolution of the lexicon: a probabilistic point of view (2510.22220)
pitch: Single HTML file: simulate two 'sister languages' diverging from a shared 100-word Swadesh list under a stochastic replacement process (Poisson clock per word) plus optional gradual-modification process. User sets true split time and replacement rate; the tool runs many Monte Carlo trials and shows the *distribution* of estimated split times from naive counting, visually proving the paper's point that point-estimates from small word lists have huge, often-ignored variance — and that adding the second process narrows the histogram.
discussion_why: decision-theory: it's a clean, self-contained lesson in 'small-N variance masquerading as precision' that maps directly onto reading too much into small poker/betting samples

title: Can an AI Out-Persuade a Human Insurance Salesman?
paper: 2609.01188 PersuaRL (RL multi-expert persuasive dialogue for insurance)
pitch: Head-to-head video: a PersuaRL-style bot vs a real insurance/warranty salesperson pitching the same product to blind testers, scored on persuasiveness and trust.
discussion_why: wins on surprise — audiences love a 'can the AI actually out-sell a human' reveal

title: Spot the Misleading Stat Pack
paper: 2608.17960 COMA compositional misleading attack + CCD defense
pitch: Single-file HTML game: present three individually TRUE sports stats (e.g. team record vs winning teams, recent ATS run, injury report) whose composition implies a false conclusion about tonight's line, and have the player identify the misleading inference before time runs out — a direct, playable version of COMA's 'every document is factually correct yet the composition misleads' trick.
discussion_why: wins on relatability — 'stats that are each true but combine to lie' is the exact fight that happens in every sports betting Discord daily

title: Pick Auditor
paper: 2608.17960 COMA compositional misleading attack + CCD defense
pitch: A leave-one-out 'Causal Counterfactual Defense' auditor for RAG-based sports/poker research assistants: before you trust an AI's pick, it shows which single source's removal would flip the recommendation, flagging picks propped up by one low-credibility doc.
discussion_why: wins on fit — bettors already obsess over 'why did the model actually like this side,' this makes that auditable

title: TrustRAG
paper: 2608.17960 COMA compositional misleading attack + CCD defense
pitch: Audit-as-a-service that runs CCD-style causal influence analysis over any RAG pipeline (betting models, security tools, financial research bots) and certifies that no single low-credibility source is dominating an output before it ships.
discussion_why: wins on surprise for AI-infra buyers, but it's a B2B pitch with limited betting/poker banter value

title: Secretary Problem Playground
paper: 2607.02150 Tight Lower Bounds for the Multi-Secretary Problem via Bellman Certificates
pitch: Single-file HTML/canvas simulator of the multi-secretary (optimal stopping) problem: drag a slider to open a gap in the value distribution and watch the regret curve visibly bend from O(log T) to O((log T)^2) in real time, run thousands of simulated 'hires' client-side — makes the paper's tight lower bound viscerally visible.
discussion_why: wins on fit with decision-theory/poker — 'when do you stop and commit' is the eternal argument in bankroll management, dating, and hiring alike

title: Key Numbers as Bellman Certificates
paper: 2607.02150 Tight Lower Bounds for the Multi-Secretary Problem via Bellman Certificates
pitch: A visualizer connecting the paper's core insight (support gaps in the value distribution force extra log-factor regret) directly to NFL 'key numbers' (3, 7) where win-probability mass clusters with gaps between — show how the same math that ruins secretary-problem regret explains why sportsbooks defend certain lines so hard.
discussion_why: wins on surprise — connecting an abstract Bellman-certificate proof to the very real, very argued-about NFL key-number phenomenon is a genuine 'wait, really?' moment

title: The Secretary Problem, But It's Tinder and the Final Table
paper: 2607.02150 Tight Lower Bounds for the Multi-Secretary Problem via Bellman Certificates
pitch: Explainer connecting the classic secretary/optimal-stopping problem to dating apps and poker tournament min-cash decisions, building up to the paper's punchline that distribution gaps (not just capacity) are what make stopping problems provably harder.
discussion_why: wins on relatability — everyone has a hot take on 'when to stop swiping' or 'when to fold for the min-cash'

title: Cap-Space Secretary
paper: 2607.02150 Tight Lower Bounds for the Multi-Secretary Problem via Bellman Certificates
pitch: An optimal-stopping simulator calibrated to NBA free agency/trade-deadline decisions (capacity = cap space, arrivals = available players), showing GMs how threshold policies with distributional gaps (star-or-bust markets) suffer the extra log-factor regret proven in the paper.
discussion_why: wins on fit — NBA front-office 'should we have waited' arguments map directly onto a provable regret bound

title: Degree Game Arena
pitch: Single-page HTML/canvas toy: you play Breaker against an AI Maker on graphs you draw yourself, watching the minimum-degree counter update live and a red line marking the proven 1/3 bound so you can see if you beat the theorem's own AI.
discussion_why: Wins on 'can you beat the math' challenge appeal — a claiming game with a hard guaranteed floor invites people to try to break it.

title: Snake Draft Is a Maker-Breaker Degree Game
pitch: Build a fantasy-draft simulator that reframes snake drafts as a Maker-Breaker degree game: each GM 'claims' player-edges, and the 1/3 bound gives a provable floor on your worst-case roster quality regardless of draft slot — with a tool showing exactly how bad your draft position can hurt you.
discussion_why: Direct hit on fantasy-sports relatability plus the surprise that draft-slot disadvantage is mathematically bounded, not doom.

title: The Game You Can't Lose by More Than 2/3
pitch: Short explainer on Maker-Breaker degree games: why the second player (Breaker), who never gets to pick first, can still lock in a third of every vertex's connections — with the 'virtual balancing' trick animated as a strategy walkthrough.
discussion_why: Niche but satisfying 'going-second-isn't-losing' surprise for a game-theory-curious audience.

title: Three Curves, One Point
pitch: Interactive HTML toy with three draggable plane curves — as you move them, the app finds the extremal-distance point pair and draws the three normal/perpendicular lines, showing them snap into concurrency (or parallel) right before your eyes, proving the paper's theorem visually.
discussion_why: Whimsical 'wait, those three lines always meet?' surprise carries it more than any betting/game tie-in.

title: Billiard-Normal Puzzle Game
pitch: Turn the curve-normal-concurrency result into a mini-golf/optics puzzle game: players shape three curved walls so a ball's optimal bounce path threads a target, using the theorem as the underlying physics engine for 'always-solvable' level generation.
discussion_why: Whimsy-driven: turning an abstract geometry theorem into a playable minigolf level generator is a delightful surprise.

title: Why These Three Invisible Lines Always Meet
pitch: Visual explainer animating optimal segments between plane curves, revealing the hidden concurrency of normals at critical points and unifying two classic tangency/perpendicularity puzzles into one picture.
discussion_why: Pure math-aesthetic surprise, limited crossover appeal beyond geometry fans.

title: Hide & Seek: Threshold Detective
pitch: Playable browser game: a target hops between two hidden sites via a Markov chain; you're the searcher choosing which site to check each round under a search-cost/imperfect-detection model, and the app scores your intuition against the provably optimal threshold-on-belief bot in real time.
discussion_why: Direct decision-theory/poker fit (reading a moving target under uncertainty) plus the 'wait, it's always just one number to compare against?' surprise.

title: Scouting-Bandwidth Line Watcher
pitch: Build a SharpLab tool that applies the proven threshold-optimal policy to a real constraint: with limited API/scouting bandwidth, which of two live games/lines do you monitor for CLV-worthy moves each tick, using belief-updating on where the value currently sits.
discussion_why: Immediately actionable for a betting-ops workflow — 'which line do you actually watch' is a live argument on any sharp-betting Discord.

title: The Math of Catching a Cheater Who Keeps Switching Hiding Spots
pitch: Explainer framing Ross's conjecture as catching a cheater alternating between two hiding spots: dramatize the belief-updating searcher and reveal that, no matter the cost/detection parameters, the optimal rule collapses to a single threshold.
discussion_why: Whimsical cheater-catching framing plus a genuine 'no way it's that simple' payoff for a decision-theory crowd.

title: Salem Number Golf
pitch: A browser leaderboard/puzzle where users hunt for the smallest-degree Salem number with a given negative trace, plotting their finds against the paper's T²/log T and T² log T bound curves — a math-golf competition made visual.
discussion_why: Niche math-puzzle whimsy — 'beat the bound' competitive framing for number-theory hobbyists, not a broad crowd-pleaser.

title: The Numbers That Almost Live on the Unit Circle
pitch: Explainer on Salem numbers — algebraic integers with all-but-one conjugate riding the unit circle — tying negative trace to the new polynomial (not exponential) degree bounds, and linking to Lehmer's problem and hyperbolic volumes.
discussion_why: Pure number-theory appeal; low crossover into game/betting discussion.

title: Salem Bound Verifier
pitch: Small in-browser tool using a JS big-integer/root-finding library to search for and verify minimal-degree Salem numbers against a target trace, letting number-theory hobbyists test the paper's bounds on real examples.
discussion_why: Useful research utility but appeals to a narrow specialist audience.

title: Cross-Market Momentum Signals
pitch: Extend the paper's price-only graph-learning momentum model beyond futures to sports-betting markets: learn spillover networks purely from historical line movement across correlated games/props (no need for hand-coded correlations) and sell the resulting momentum signal as a CLV-timing feed.
discussion_why: High-stakes econ/betting fit — 'can price momentum spread between unrelated markets predict line moves' is exactly the kind of claim a sharp-betting Discord will fight about.

title: NBA Props Network Momentum Pipeline
pitch: Feed SharpLab's odds history into a linear, interpretable graph-learning model (mirroring the paper's futures setup) to detect momentum spillover between correlated NBA lines/props, and backtest whether front-running the spillover beats closing line value.
discussion_why: Concrete extension of David's own live betting stack — a real backtest result ('does it beat CLV') is guaranteed to spark argument.

title: Watch Momentum Spread Like Wildfire
pitch: Animated network visualization: nodes are the 64 futures contracts (or any asset universe you swap in), edges are learned momentum-spillover weights, and a playback slider shows momentum literally propagating across the graph day by day, 2000-2022.
discussion_why: Visually mesmerizing 'contagion' animation, though less directly argument-starting than the trading-strategy angle.

title: Momentum Is Contagious: How Price Trends Jump Between Markets
pitch: Explainer using the animated momentum-network visualization to walk through how a purely price-based graph model uncovers hidden spillover between commodities, equities, bonds, and currencies — and what a 1.5 Sharpe, 22% annual return strategy built on it actually means.
discussion_why: Strong econ surprise ('no fundamental data needed') with broad appeal to a betting/trading-adjacent audience.

title: Sportsbook Market-Maker Simulator
paper: 2307.01816 — OTC Market Making via Reinforcement Learning
pitch: Single-page HTML toy where you play bookmaker: incoming 'bettors' arrive with an order-arrival intensity that falls off as you widen the spread (the paper's core linear intensity-vs-spread assumption), and you choose spreads each tick while an inventory/liability meter tracks your exposure. A toggle overlays the paper's closed-form optimal Gaussian spread policy against your manual choices and a naive 'always-widen' bot, plotting P&L and terminal inventory risk across game-time-remaining. Directly visualizes why real books shade lines late in games or when one side is overloaded.
discussion_why: wins on 'wait really' surprise — it exposes bookmaking as literally the market-making math from quant finance, which is catnip for a betting/decision-theory Discord.

title: RL Liquidity Bot for Prediction Markets
paper: 2307.01816 — OTC Market Making via Reinforcement Learning
pitch: Adapt the paper's inventory-aware, size-dependent spread policy into an automated market-maker for Polymarket/Kalshi/Betfair-style exchanges — quoting two-sided odds on illiquid markets (props, futures, niche politics) and dynamically re-pricing based on order flow and current inventory risk, the same problem OTC dealers solve for bonds. Prediction markets are exploding and thin books are the biggest complaint; a tuned RL quoting engine is a real edge business, not just a toy.
discussion_why: wins on betting/econ fit — it's a concrete 'could this actually make money' business debate for a gambling-savvy crowd.

title: Why Sportsbooks Widen Lines Late — The RL Market-Maker Explainer
paper: 2307.01816 — OTC Market Making via Reinforcement Learning
pitch: A 10-minute explainer that walks from Avellaneda-Stoikov-style market making to this paper's OTC/RL twist, using screen-capture of the Sportsbook Simulator demo above to show live how spreads should balloon as inventory or time-to-close moves against the house — reframing 'the book is scared of that side' as literal optimal control math.
discussion_why: wins on relatability — every bettor has a theory about why lines move, this gives them the actual math to argue about.

title: Cross-Modal NBA Embedding Aligner
paper: 2602.16584 — The Representational Alignment Hypothesis
pitch: Precompute embeddings of NBA players from three modalities (box-score stat vectors, a text embedding of scouting-report style descriptions, and a CLIP embedding of headshots), bake them into a static HTML page, and let a slider fit + animate a learned linear (Procrustes) map between spaces, showing nearest-neighbor accuracy climb as you align — a hands-on demo of the paper's claim that independently trained embeddings share near-isomorphic geometry.
discussion_why: wins on surprise — most people don't expect a stat line and a face photo to land in 'the same shape' of space after one linear map.

title: The Vibe Translator (Platonic Space Satire Machine)
paper: 2602.16584 — The Representational Alignment Hypothesis
pitch: A whimsical single-file toy: type unhinged poker table-talk or bad-beat trash talk, it embeds the text, applies a (deliberately overclaimed) 'universal linear map' into a fake 'player-performance embedding space' and 'wine-tasting-note space,' spitting out absurd cross-modal 'translations' — a gentle send-up of the paper's own caution against over-reading the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, while still being a genuinely fun toy.
discussion_why: wins on whimsy — it's a delightfully dumb toy that also smuggles in a real epistemology debate about whether AI models are converging on 'one true representation of reality.'

title: Is There a Platonic Space Behind Every AI Model?
paper: 2602.16584 — The Representational Alignment Hypothesis
pitch: Explainer connecting this paper to the broader 'Platonic Representation Hypothesis' conversation, using a live demo (align CLIP image embeddings to word2vec via one linear map, show nearest-neighbor recall) to make the abstract claim tangible, then walking through the paper's actual pushback against the strongest 'one true reality' reading.
discussion_why: wins on surprise — 'different AIs trained on totally different data land in the same shape of space' is a legitimate mind-bender for a general audience.

title: GTO-to-Language Alignment Prober
paper: 2602.16584 — The Representational Alignment Hypothesis
pitch: Test the paper's hypothesis on a poker-native dataset: take a solver's numeric strategy vectors (frequencies across a range) for a set of spots and an LLM's text embeddings of natural-language descriptions of the same spots, then check via representational similarity analysis / linear alignment whether the solver's 'geometry of good play' and the language model's 'geometry of poker concepts' are near-isomorphic — a real research mini-project with a poker audience hook.
discussion_why: wins on poker fit — 'does the AI's map of GTO play look like how humans talk about poker' is a debate poker nerds will actually have opinions on.

title: The Weirdest CV Paper This Week: Tracking Wild Horses From a Drone
paper: 2603.03604 — Tracking Feral Horses in Aerial Video Using Oriented Bounding Boxes
pitch: Fun explainer on the head/tail ambiguity problem in oriented-bounding-box tracking (why a horse's rotated box can silently flip 180 degrees between frames) and the paper's cute fix — three separate head/tail/combined detectors voting by IoU to hit 99.3% accuracy — then riffs on where else the trick applies: broadcast top-down shots of NFL formations, poker dealers' hands, or pool-table overhead cams.
discussion_why: wins on whimsy/surprise — a drone-vs-feral-horses CV paper is an instant 'wait, what' hook before the pivot to sports/poker applications.

title: Orientation-Flip Voting Toy
paper: 2603.03604 — Tracking Feral Horses in Aerial Video Using Oriented Bounding Boxes
pitch: A self-contained HTML/canvas visualization of synthetic rotated ellipses ('horses') with an ambiguous head/tail marker, showing frame-by-frame how a naive single detector flips orientation randomly while the paper's 3-detector IoU-majority-vote scheme stabilizes it — a clean, no-backend teaching demo of the actual algorithmic trick, no real video model required.
discussion_why: wins on buildability with mild surprise — it's a satisfying 'aha, that's the whole trick' toy rather than a debate-starter.

title: Feral Horse Fantasy League
paper: 2603.03604 — Tracking Feral Horses in Aerial Video Using Oriented Bounding Boxes
pitch: Pair live/recorded aerial drone footage of real feral horse herds (Assateague, Outer Banks, Australian brumbies) with individual-horse tracking from this paper's method, then let people 'draft' individual horses and wager on which one leads the herd, wins a skirmish, or survives migration longest — a genuinely novel gambling/fantasy-sports product built entirely on a niche CV paper.
discussion_why: wins on whimsy+gambling combo — 'you can bet on wild horses via drone AI tracking' is the kind of absurd-but-real pitch that gets argued about for an hour.

title: Galled Network Phase-Transition Playground
paper: 2608.20860 — A cube-root phase transition in tree-child networks
pitch: Interactive d3 force-graph demo: pick n (leaves) and k (reticulations) via sliders, generate a random tree-child network, and watch a live readout classify it as 'semi-simplex' or not, with a marker showing where k crosses the n^(1/3) threshold — and a second panel showing the enumeration formula silently diverging from the true count once k passes that line, versus staying accurate out to n^(1/2) for plain tree-child/normal networks.
discussion_why: wins on 'wait really' math surprise — watching a clean formula visibly break at a specific, unexpected exponent is inherently nerd-snipey.

title: The Cube-Root Rule: A Hidden Threshold in Nature's Family Trees
paper: 2608.20860 — A cube-root phase transition in tree-child networks
pitch: Explainer tying this paper's n^(1/3) enumeration-breakdown threshold to other famous sqrt/cube-root phase transitions (giant-component critical window in Erdos-Renyi random graphs, birthday paradox), using the Galled Network Playground demo as the visual centerpiece, aimed at a general math-curious audience.
discussion_why: wins on surprise — most viewers have never heard that phylogenetic network counting has its own critical exponent, distinct from the usual sqrt(n) thresholds.

title: When Does Your Parlay Tree Stop Being a Tree?
paper: 2608.20860 — A cube-root phase transition in tree-child networks
pitch: A provocative stretch-demo/discussion piece: model a correlated same-game parlay as a 'reticulated tree' where each cross-leg correlation is a reticulation edge, and argue by analogy to the paper's threshold that once correlated legs exceed roughly the cube root of your total leg count, naive independent-probability multiplication (what most books' parlay calculators implicitly assume) starts to diverge sharply from the true joint probability — a fun, half-serious framework for why some parlay pricing feels 'off.'
discussion_why: wins on betting fit — it turns an obscure phylogenetics threshold into direct ammunition for the 'are correlated parlays systematically mispriced' argument every betting Discord has.

title: Multi-City SIR + Migration + Cure-Timing Simulator
paper: 2510.25085 — Explorations of Epidemiological Dynamics across Multiple Population Hubs
pitch: Self-contained HTML/canvas simulator: a handful of 'cities' connected by migration edges, each running an SIR-with-cure model; sliders control migration rate and per-city cure-release timing, live charts show how a delayed cure in one hub cascades into higher mortality across the whole connected network — directly visualizing the paper's core theoretical + numerical result.
discussion_why: wins on buildability — pure client-side ODE simulation with charts, ships tonight with zero backend, and the 'cascading consequences of one city's delay' result is inherently shareable.

title: Pandemic Bookie
paper: 2510.25085 — Explorations of Epidemiological Dynamics across Multiple Population Hubs
pitch: Turn the multi-hub SIR simulator into a betting game: players wager virtual chips on which city peaks first, which city has the highest death toll, or whether an early vs. late cure release in the hub city saves more lives network-wide — the epidemiological model becomes 'the house,' resolving bets after each simulated run, playable solo or as a Discord activity.
discussion_why: wins on the games+gambling+whimsy combo — betting on a simulated pandemic is exactly the kind of morbidly fun mechanic that gets a Discord arguing about strategy for an evening.

title: We Simulated Releasing a Cure Early vs. Late Across Cities
paper: 2510.25085 — Explorations of Epidemiological Dynamics across Multiple Population Hubs
pitch: Short data-driven explainer built around screen-capture of the Multi-City SIR Simulator, running side-by-side 'early cure' vs 'late cure' scenarios and narrating how migration between hubs amplifies or dampens the timing decision's impact — a concrete, watchable version of the paper's abstract policy takeaway.
discussion_why: wins on relatability — 'when should you release the cure' is an intuitive policy dilemma anyone can have an opinion on after watching the simulation play out.
